It was generally thought, upon this event, that the Tory party would have had the ascendant: but, contrary to all expectation, the Whigs had managed matters fo well as to yet entirely into the queen's confidence, and to have the whole administration of affairs in their hands. Swift's friends were now in power; and the Whigs in general, knowing him to be the author of the Difcouffe on the Contells, &e, which was written in defence of King William and his minifiers against the violent proceedings of the house of commons, confidered themselves as much obliged to him, and looked upon him as fail to their party. But Swift thought with the Whigs only in the flat ; for with respect to the church his principles were always those of a Tony. He therefore declined any intimate connection with the leaders of the party, who at that time profelled what was called _low church principles_. But what above all hocked him, fays Mr Sheridan, was their inviting Delits, Freethinkers, Atheists, Jews, and Infields to be of their party, under pretence of moderation, and allowing a general liberty of conference. As Swift was in his heart a man of true religion, he could not have borne, even in his private character, to have mixed with such a motely crew. But when we confer his principles in his political capacity, that he looked upon the church of England, as by law established, to be the main pillar of our newly erected confirmation, he could not, confilently with the character of a good citizen, join with those who considered it more as an ornament than a support to the edifice; and could therefore look on with compofore while it was undermining, or could even open the gate to a blind multitude, to try, like Sampfon, their strength again if, and confident it only as part.
